newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Korea's "big bang" just getting started - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Korea's "big bang" just getting started - analysts.

text.p: The first phase of South Korea's financial reforms was hardly the "big bang" markets were promised, but the stage has been set for more meaningful reforms in the future, economists said on Wednesday.

Unofficially released on Tuesday, the 18-point plan of the Presidential Commission for Financial Reform would generally free banks and non-bank financial institutions to engage in more kinds of business.
"It is not a big bang," said Kim Kyeong-won, head of research at Samsung Securities Co.
"But even if this committee fails to implement its reforms, the alternatives they propose will be there so that the government can fully implement them later."
Hahm Joon-ho, one of 15 economists advising the commission, said a "big bang", which refers to Britain's financial reforms of 1986, can begin with small moves towards deregulation.
"This could be the start of Korea's big bang. We are continuing to work on more fundamental and structural reforms that will be announced later in the year," Hahm said.
The plan barely addresses its most controversial task: deciding whether South Korea's top five business groups, or chaebols, should be allowed to run banks.
Chaebol are banned from owning banks to prevent an even greater concentration of power in an economy dominated by a few industrial giants.

Some economists have urged an end to the ban to create more efficient management at Korean banks and insulate them from the kind of political meddling that led to a loans scandal involving Hanbo Steel Co.
The steelmaking flagship of the nation's 14th largest chaebol collapsed in January, revealing a web of corruption linking company officials, bankers and politicians.

"Why shouldn't chaebol own banks?" said Samsung's Kim. "Banks are the weakest link of the financial industry because they are not really owned by anyone. Everybody is an owner and nobody is an owner." In the first phase of reforms, commission members have recommended that each of the top five chaebols be allowed one non-permanent directorship on the board of one bank.
Chaebols will not be allowed on the board of any bank with which they have substantial outstanding loans.
"This was symbolic rather than meaningful," Kim said.
Commission adviser Hahm said the issue was "very, very sensitive".
Commission members agreed to limited chaebol participation in bank management, Hahm said, but decided to study further the question of chaebol ownership of banks.

"In the first phase or short-term plan, we recommended reforms we knew could be implemented right away. We will make recommendations on more fundamental and structural reforms at the end of June," Hahm said.

The commission is to present the plan for first-stage reforms to President Kim Young-sam next week. The plan then will be turned over to the Ministry of Finance and Economy for implementation, which is scheduled for later this year.
Commission members, mainly academics and business people, plans two more rounds of recommendations for longer-term financial reforms in the second half of the year, Hahm said.

"There is potential for these reforms to result in something meaningful," said an analyst with a Korean securities firm who asked not to be identified. "But there have been other committees that suggested reforms in the past. Nothing happened."
